Ranking one positive against 99 negatives measures performance within that sampled candidate set. Krichene and Rendle show sampled ranking metrics can reverse model ordering relative to full-catalog metrics, even in expectation. For this benchmark, preserve the pinned evaluator and interpret HR@10 gains as improvements under its specific protocol; they do not establish better full-catalog recommendations. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

Recommended uncertainty diagnostic: retain each model’s per-user binary hit indicators and bootstrap their paired differences, resampling the same user indices for both models. Resample 200 users within each category, then average the four category differences equally; report the observed macro difference and a 95% bootstrap interval. Pairing preserves shared-user dependence, as described in [SciPy’s bootstrap documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html). One additional hit changes category HR by 0.005 and the four-category macro average by 0.00125. These intervals describe user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the trained models and fixed candidates; they exclude training-seed and negative-sampling uncertainty.

Repeated adaptive hyperparameter selection can overfit finite validation data: the winning validation score becomes optimistic, potentially by amounts comparable to algorithm differences. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) establish this selection-bias problem. Practical implication: record all trials, inspect paired differences and category consistency, and treat tiny selected gains cautiously. A bootstrap interval computed after choosing the winner does not correct adaptive selection bias. Keep hidden test data untouched and reserve held-out evaluation for the final selected model.
